A_target.statement:
Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be [[Definition:Square-Integrable Random Variable|square-integrable]] [[Definition:Random Variable|random variables]] with $\cov {X_i, X_j} = 0$ for $i \ne j$.
Then:
:$\displaystyle \var {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n X_i} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \var {X_i}$

B_source.statement:
Let $\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_n$ be pairwise [[Definition:Orthogonal (Inner Product Space)|orthogonal]] vectors in an [[Definition:Inner Product Space|inner product space]].
Then:
:$\displaystyle \norm {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \mathbf v_i}^2 = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \norm {\mathbf v_i}^2$

substitutions.vector space of vectors: space of mean-zero L^2 random variables

validity_conditions: Mean-zero L^2 random variables form a real inner product space with <X,Y> = Cov(X,Y); variance is the squared norm.
Uncorrelated = orthogonal in this space, so the Pythagorean cross-term cancellation transfers verbatim.
Centering (subtracting means) is WLOG since variance is translation-invariant.
proof_plan: Model the centred variables $Y_i = X_i - \expect {X_i}$ as vectors in $\map {L^2} \Pr$ with $\innerprod {Y_i} {Y_j} = \cov {X_i, X_j}$.
As the variables are uncorrelated, the cross terms vanish; that is, the $Y_i$ are [[Definition:Orthogonal (Inner Product Space)|orthogonal]].

Hence:
:$\displaystyle \var {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n X_i} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \var {X_i}$
which is [[Pythagoras's Theorem (Inner Product Space)|the Pythagorean identity]] in $\map {L^2} \Pr$.
{{qed}}
